title.narrative: Preparing the set-up of a Fruit Processing Facility for Kapok Fibre in Indonesia

description.narrative: Kapok fibres, also known as Silk Cotton or Java Cotton, is 100% organic, biodegradable and recyclable and can be used as a sustainable alternative to cotton in the Clothing industry. Indonesia delivers the best quality Kapok in the world and is one of the largest producers with 50 million kilograms of fibres per year. The trees flourish in dry soil and barely need water, herewith preventing corrosion and reducing CO2 emissions. Despite these sustainable qualities, the Kapok industry in Indonesia has not innovated in the past 100 years and current production methods and quality of these fibres are not sustainable and are insufficient yet to meet demand from the clothing industry. Dutch company Flocus B.V., with a background in textile engineering and already supplying clothes made of kapok to some of the largest premium clothing brands, wants to set-up the first environment-friendly sorting facility for Kapok and help revolutionise the industry. To prepare for future investments in a certified Kapok Sorting Facility in Indonesia for the processing of Kapok Fibres, Technical Assistance (DGGF) provided support for a Technical Feasibility Study. The project included assessing the legal set-up of the facility, location selection, a technical study for machine selection and factory lay-out and a supply chain analysis. The project has been successful as has resulted in a viable business plan to attract further investment of the Kapok facility which is expected to open in 2020. Investments in product development for industrial purposes of Kapok and the set-up of a Farm are also being explored and further scale-up activities should take place within 3-5 years. These investments could lead to at least 15-25 direct jobs per facility, 100-500 seasonal jobs during harvest seasons and considerably higher incomes for Kapok farmers in the supply chain. Furthermore, the investments are likely to contribute to the stabilisation of the Kapok market, prevent deforestation and help regenerate entire eco-systems and enable existing industries to become more sustainable.
